_about: Per-pick operation cycle of a single-lift, single-cylinder Jacquard on a treadle hand loom, as one master scalar phi in [0, 1). Each move names a node from component_inventory.csv and the scalar it drives. The ORDER of events is documented; the hand-loom FRACTIONS are derived from Bradbury's measured power-loom timing (kept verbatim in 'documented_reference') and stretched to give the weaver a longer open-shed dwell, so they are estimates. Source keys: see ../sources/notes-mechanism.md.

master_scalar.name: phi
master_scalar.zero: treadle starts down = griffe starts to rise (Bradbury crank 55 deg)
master_scalar.picks_per_minute_basis: est (no period hand-Jacquard figure found; power single-lift 90-140)

hole_means.value: HOLE = needle not moved = hook stays over its knife = hook, harness and warp end LIFTED. BLANK = needle pushed = hook off the knife = warp end stays DOWN.
hole_means.evidence: Posselt pp. 14-15: a blank card pushes all hooks off ('empty lift'); an empty cylinder or fully cut card lifts every hook. Barlow p. 150: 'wherever a perforation was made opposite to a needle, then the corresponding hook would be raised'. Bradbury p. 75: fully perforated card lifts all, blank leaves all down. Bell (Verdol paper): uncut paper raises the feeler and hitting wire, which pushes the needle back.

what_is_cut_from_the_design.value: Design (point) paper: by common practice painted squares = warp up (Barlow Fig. 149: black = warp), so the cutter punches the painted squares. But the cutter may be told to cut the blank squares instead (Bell: for a double-cloth tie the first half of the card is cut on the coloured squares and the second half on the blank squares), and Posselt labels designs either 'figure up' or 'ground up' / 'warp up' or 'filling up'.
what_is_cut_from_the_design.note: So the paint convention varies by mill and fabric; the machine convention (hole = lift) does not. The simulator should fix: 1 = warp up = hole.

reading_order.value: First card (first pick) cut from the bottom line of the design; each card read from the first hook; first hook usually reckoned from the left at the front of the loom, but some districts reckon from the back, which makes the cutter read from the top right.

empty_cylinder.value: With no card, needles enter the cylinder holes and every hook is lifted.

single_vs_double_lift_shed.value: Single lift: closed (bottom-closed) shed - all lifted hooks return to the bottom every pick. Double lift: semi-open shed - a warp end up on consecutive picks meets the other griffe half-way (Posselt counts 8 vs 14 movements for 7 picks up in an 8-leaf satin).

documented_reference.where: Ch. VII, 'Timing the various movements in Single Lift Jacquards', pp. 80-82, Fig. 74 (crank circle in 12 divisions of 30 deg)
documented_reference.conditions: Single-lift Jacquard on a 5/4 single-shuttle power loom at 120 picks/min; griffe driven by a crank on the top shaft set about 35 deg behind the loom crank; card cylinder driven independently by an eccentric. Crank angle 0 = top centre, loom at rest, shed closed, griffe at the bottom.
documented_reference.ocr_note: Table and text checked against the page image (archive.org jacquardmechanis00brad, leaf n87 = p. 82); durations sum to 360 deg.
documented_reference.phi_mapping: phi = ((crank_deg - 55) mod 360) / 360, so phi = 0 when the griffe starts to rise

events.event: cylinder leaves the needles (end of 40 deg contact dwell)
cylinder half turned (45 deg, on a corner)
griffe at top: shed fully open
cylinder at the limit of its outward travel, turned 90 deg
griffe starts to fall (end of top dwell)
cylinder starts back towards the needles
griffe reaches rest at the bottom

phases.name: Treadle down: knives take the selected hooks

moves.motion: rotate about its heel pivot (deg)
rotate (deg); outer end pulled down by the cord
translate +Z (mm)
translate +Z with the griffe once the knife is under the crook

still: cylinder.batten (card still pressed on the needles)
phases.description: The card that was pressed in at the end of the previous pick holds the blanked needles back, so their hooks stay clear of the knives. The knives rise, pass the pushed-back crooks and catch under the crooks of the hooks whose needles went into holes. The cylinder must not leave before this.
phases.evidence: Bradbury p. 78: no slide movement 'until the bowl a reaches the angle formed in the swan neck. This affords sufficient time for the knives to reach and catch under the hooks'. Bradbury timing: contact dwell lasts to crank 70 deg, griffe rises from 55 deg.

phases.name: Griffe rises, shed opens; cylinder swings out and turns one face

moves.motion: rotate (deg)
rotate (deg)
translate +Z (mm)
translate +Z (mm)
moves.note: hook rises with the knife; unselected hooks stay on the bottom board

moves.motion: translate +Z with the hook (mm)
mail end of the warp rises; shed opens
swing about the top centre pins (angle) or slide (mm)
spring returns every pushed needle forward once the card leaves (mm)
tilt back to vertical with its needle (deg)
moves.note: the knives are already above the crooks, so they are not caught

moves.motion: rotate about its own axis (deg), only after the lantern meets the top catch (from phi 0.15)
moves.note: hammer pressed down by the lantern corner, then snaps back on the next flat

moves.motion: translate along its guide (mm): pushed by the lantern corner and returned by its spring
ride on the cylinder: the used card moves off the needle face, the next one comes round to it

phases.description: Selected hooks, their harness cords, mails and lingoes rise. The cylinder is thrown out by the bowl in the S-iron, meets the top catch and is turned a quarter turn, bringing the next card to the needle face.
phases.basis: doc (order) / derived (fractions from Bradbury, shortened rise for a hand loom)
phases.evidence: Bradbury pp. 74-76: as the head rises the swing frame carries the cylinder away; 'the catch 42 holds against the top corner of the cylinder ... causes the cylinder 32 to rotate'; 45 deg at mid-travel, 90 deg at the end. Barlow p. 152: pulley on the griffe slides in an S bar. Posselt p. 15: batten 'thrown outwards' when the guiding rod rises.

phases.name: Shed held open: batten back, shuttle thrown

moves.motion: rotate about its pivot (deg): pushed back towards the harness
translate across the race (mm), box to box
laid in the shed behind the shuttle

still: cylinder.batten out, next card facing the needles
phases.description: The weaver holds the treadle down, pushes the batten back to clear the shed in front of the reed and throws (or picks) the shuttle through.
phases.evidence: Barlow pp. 83-84 (common fly-shuttle hand loom): push the batten back a few inches, throw the shuttle, draw the batten forward.

phases.name: Beat-up

moves.motion: rotate toward the cloth fell and back (deg)
with the sley

phases.description: The batten is drawn forward and the reed beats the new pick against the fell. In Barlow's hand-loom description the beat comes before the shed is changed; power-loom Jacquards are set so the shed is level (crossing) when the reed is about 1 1/2 in from the cloth.
alternatives: beat on the closing shed (power-loom setting, NELSON1909, double-action section: 'reed about 1 1/2 inches from the cloth when the shed is level')

phases.name: Treadle released: griffe falls, shed closes; next card pressed in

moves.motion: rotate back (deg)
rotate back (deg)
translate -Z (mm), pulled down by lingoes, hooks and harness
descend with the knives and land on the bottom board
return to the race
settle to rest (deg)
swing back toward the needle board (mm)
pushed back against its spring (mm) when the card arrives, at phi about 0.91
tilt back with its needle (deg) so its crook clears the knife

moves.node: hooks.hook.N (still vertical, not lifted last pick)
moves.motion: deflected back by the inclined knife face as the knife passes below the crook, then springs over it

phases.description: Releasing the treadle lets the weight of the lingoes and harness pull the griffe down. The S-iron brings the cylinder in, and the next card meets the needles shortly before the griffe lands: holes let needles through into the cylinder holes (hook stays over its knife), blanks push needles and hooks back off the knives.
phases.evidence: Barlow p. 157: 'the card strikes the needles before the hooks have landed upon the bottom board'; also the inclined face of the descending griffe bars forces unpushed hooks back until the bars pass below the crooks. Bradbury: contact at crank 30 deg, griffe rest at 40 deg.

phases.name: Rest: selection set; take-up when needed

moves.motion: rotate (deg) by hand through the ratchet, every few picks
rotate (deg) over one ratchet tooth

still: cylinder.batten in, card on the needles
phases.description: Closed shed, all warp on the race, card pressed: the machine is ready for the next treadle stroke. On a hand loom the cloth is wound on by hand (ratchet, pawl and handle); Posselt notes reserve hooks were sometimes used for 'guiding the take-up motion on hand-looms'.

faults.fault: Lost pick (shuttle not thrown or weft broke while the card advanced)
faults.effect: That design line is missing from the cloth.
faults.remedy: Pull the reverse cord: the top catch is lifted and the bottom catch engages, so the cylinder turns backwards on the next lift; turn back to the right card and weave on.

faults.effect: Cards are presented in reverse order, one face back per pick, so the design is woven mirror-wise in the weft direction. Used on purpose to find a lost pick and to reverse the cards for bordered goods.

faults.fault: Card caught on the needle points / thrown off the pegs (warped or damp cards, cylinder too close when turning)
faults.effect: 'pick-out': wrong or no selection; cards can be torn and new holes punched by the pegs.

faults.fault: Cylinder half-turned (stops on a corner) when the lay is pushed back by hand
faults.effect: The corner strikes and bends needle points down; some hooks that should rise do not and some that should not do. The spring protecting catch prevents it.
Needles strike the card margins: wrong lifts. Test by greasing the needle heads and reading the marks on a card (Posselt Fig. XVI).

faults.fault: Cylinder not pressed close enough to the needle board
faults.effect: Hooks not pushed far enough from the knives: blanked hooks are lifted anyway (wrong shed).

faults.fault: Needle eye or hook out of line
faults.effect: Hook out of the vertical; the falling knife can land on the hook top ('crowned' hooks).

faults.fault: Double-cylinder machine: one cylinder gets a pick ahead
faults.effect: Cards out of rotation; twill broken up. Single-cylinder machines avoid this, which is why the silk trade kept them.

toy_8_hook._about: Toy 8-hook machine: ONE cross-row of a real 8-row head - 8 knives, 8 hooks, 8 needles stacked in one vertical tier, card = one column of 8 holes between 2 peg holes. Straight tie: hook n -> warp end n.

machine.needle_to_hook_rule: needle 1 (top) -> hook nearest the needle board ... needle 8 (bottom) -> hook nearest the spring box (Nelson)

toy_8_hook.design_note: 1 = warp up (painted square). Lines are woven bottom line first. The motif is an upward arrow, deliberately not symmetric top-to-bottom so that the reading order shows. Weft floats up to 3 under, 2-4 over; real cloth adds a binding weave.
toy_8_hook.woven_cells_legend: W = warp end over the pick (warp shows on the face), f = weft (filling) over the end. Top line = last pick woven. Seen from the weaver's seat the newest pick is at the fell, farthest away, so the arrow appears upright.

plain_weave_check.note: Two cards alternated give plain (tabby) cloth: a quick test of the simulator.

with_repeating_tie.tie: 3 harness cords per neck cord; warp end e hangs on hook ((e - 1) mod 8) + 1; 24 ends
with_repeating_tie.point: 8 hooks control 24 ends: the cards are unchanged, the arrow appears 3 times across

with_point_tie.tie: 15 ends on hooks 1,2,...,8,7,...,1 (hook 8 is the single centre cord; hooks 1-7 carry 2 cords)
with_point_tie.point: a symmetric figure twice as wide as the hooks allow, from half the design (Barlow Figs. 152-153)

toy_8_hook.basis: constructed example using the documented rules

real_400_hook._about: Real case: 400-hook single-lift head, 8 rows x 50 cross-rows (+ 2 reserve cross-rows = 416 needles), straight-through repeating tie in 4 divisions (Posselt Fig. XXVIII) -> 1600 warp ends.

numbering.hook_to_card_position: hook h -> card column c = ceil(h / 8) (1..50, 51-52 reserve), needle row r = ((h - 1) mod 8) + 1
numbering.neck_cords: bottom-board row 1 carries neck cords 1-8, row 50 carries 393-400 (Posselt Fig. XXIX)
numbering.comber_board: 8 rows deep; each comber-board cross-row takes 8 consecutive ends from one hook cross-row (Norwich/English tie: row 1 of the board from neck cords 1-8, row 2 from 9-16, ...)
numbering.end_to_hook: warp end e (1..1600) -> hook ((e - 1) mod 400) + 1; each hook lifts ends h, h+400, h+800, h+1200

ground_check_8_end_satin.rule: pick p lifts every hook in needle row s = ((p - 1) x 3 mod 8) + 1, i.e. one hole in every card column: 50 holes per card, 200 of 1600 ends up
ground_check_8_end_satin.note: Posselt p. 28: 400 / 8 = 50 repeats of an 8-leaf satin; a 12-leaf satin does not divide 400, so use 396 hooks (33 repeats) or 408 (34, borrowing 8 reserve hooks).

scale_examples.case: Barlow p. 160: silk scarf, 24 in at 400 ends/in = 9600 ends, 400-needle Jacquard
scale_examples.derived: 9600 / 400 = 24 harness cords per neck cord if the figure repeats every inch (straight repeating tie)

scale_examples.case: Posselt p. 20: 100 ends/in, 36 in wide, 600 machine (12 rows)
scale_examples.derived: 3600 comber-board holes, 300 across x 12 deep; 3600 / 600 = 6 cords per neck cord

scale_examples.case: Posselt Fig. XVII: 156-card set with a hanging wire every 12th card
scale_examples.derived: a design 156 picks long needs 156 cards (one card per pick)
